title: Moore's Law and Why Performance Engineering Became Necessary
explainer: Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of components on a chip was roughly doubling every year or two powered decades of software getting faster 'for free' just by waiting for new hardware. As that doubling slowed and processor speed pulled far ahead of memory speed - a gap engineers call the memory wall - squeezing performance out of existing hardware became a skill in its own right rather than something new chips would solve for you. The hardware mechanics themselves (caches, clock speeds, chip design) belong to the Hardware & Computer Systems track; this is just the historical reason performance engineering exists as a discipline.
